title: State-space graphs
sub: Word Ladder and a path that breaks walls: a vertex is a state, and the size of the state space estimates the cost
cards/0/title: Word Ladder: a graph that isn't in memory
cards/0/body:
Word Ladder (LeetCode #127). You get beginWord, endWord and a list wordList — up to 5000 words of the same length, up to 10 lowercase Latin letters. Each step changes one letter, and every intermediate word must be in the list (the first one needn't be). Return the number of words in the shortest chain from the first word to the last, both included, or 0 if there is no chain.

Signals: “fewest steps”, and every step is a small change. That's a shortest path in an unweighted graph, i.e. level-order BFS. Vertices are words, and an edge joins words that differ in one letter.

What's new compared with a grid: the graph is not given. You have to find a word's neighbors yourself — and how you find them decides the whole cost. A vertex here is not a cell but a state of the problem; later in this lesson the state becomes composite too.
cards/1/title: Finding neighbors: all pairs or 26 letters
cards/1/body:
All pairs. Build the graph up front: compare every pair of words letter by letter. There are N²/2 pairs and a comparison is L characters: for N = 5000, L = 10 that's 5000²/2 · 10 ≈ 1.25·10⁸ — before the search even starts.

Generation. Don't look for neighbors among the words — create candidates: in each of the L positions put each of 26 letters and ask a HashSet whether such a word exists. That's L·26 candidates per word, each costing O(L): build the string and compute its hash. For the whole BFS, N · L · 26 · L = 5000 · 10 · 26 · 10 ≈ 1.3·10⁷.

The numbers decide which way wins: generation grows as N·L²·26, all pairs as N²·L. With a large list and short words (the usual case) generation wins; with a hundred long words, all pairs does.

The “visited” mark is removing the word from the set: words.Remove returns true only the first time. One set serves as both the dictionary and visited.
cards/2/q: The list has 5000 words of length 5. Roughly how much work do comparing all pairs and generating candidates take?
cards/2/options/0: ≈ 6·10⁷ and ≈ 3·10⁶: generation is about 20 times cheaper
cards/2/options/1: ≈ 2.5·10⁷ and ≈ 6.5·10⁵: word length doesn't affect the cost
cards/2/options/2: The same: both ways compare every word with every other
cards/2/explain: Pairs: 5000²/2 · 5 ≈ 6.25·10⁷ character comparisons. Generation: 5000 · 5 positions · 26 letters · 5 for the string and its hash ≈ 3.25·10⁶. The ratio of the costs is N/2 versus 26·L: 2500 versus 130, about 19 times.
cards/2/wrong/1: Length enters both costs: comparing a pair is up to L characters, and each candidate is a new string of length L that also has to be hashed.
cards/2/wrong/2: Generation doesn't compare words with each other: it builds L·26 candidates and asks the set, at O(L) each.
cards/3/body:
A plain level-order BFS from u10.l1. The level number is the number of words in the chain: the first word is level 1. Invariant: level k holds exactly the words whose shortest chain is k words long. So the moment the target word leaves the queue, its level is the answer, and there's no need to search further.

The answer is the number of words, not of transitions: one more than the edges in the path. It is a common off-by-one error.

If endWord isn't in the list, return 0 right away: you can't step into it. Remove the first word from the set if it's there — otherwise you can come back to it.

Cost: each word enters the queue once, and for each one L·26 candidates are generated at O(L) apiece — O(N·L²·26) time, O(N·L) memory for the set and the queue.
cards/4/task: Step through Word Ladder from hit to cog. One rig step is a new BFS level. The rig will ask twice what happens next.
cards/4/goal/asks/0/q: Level 2 is [hot]. What will be on level 3?
cards/4/goal/asks/0/explain: The words one letter away from hot are hit, dot and lot. dot and lot are in the list and haven't been seen yet. hit is the first word: it isn't in the list, and if it were, it would have been removed at the start — BFS must not go back to what it has covered. lot is as much a neighbor as dot: the loop tries every position, not only the first.
cards/4/goal/asks/1/q: Level 4 is [dog, log]. What does the code return?
cards/4/goal/asks/1/explain: cog is one letter away from both dog and log, so it lands on level 5, and the answer is 5: that's how many words the chain hit → hot → dot → dog → cog has. It has 4 transitions — that's exactly the off-by-one error. Going through log would give a chain of the same length: BFS answers with the level, not with a path.
cards/5/title: A state is not a cell: a path that breaks walls
cards/5/body:
Shortest Path in a Grid with Obstacles Elimination (LeetCode #1293). An m×n grid up to 40×40, 0 is empty, 1 is a wall. Go from the top-left corner to the bottom-right one in side steps; you may break at most k walls. Find the minimum number of steps or return −1.

Why visited per cell is wrong. You can arrive at a cell twice: earlier but having spent a break, and later having kept it. The second visit isn't a repeat: with breaks in reserve, paths open up that were closed to the first visit. Marking by cell throws it away, and the answer gets lost.

A vertex is a state (r, c, breaks left). A step into an empty cell keeps the reserve, a step into a wall spends one break; a reserve below zero means no move. The mark is bool[m, n, k + 1], over all three coordinates. A BFS level is one step, and the very first state in the target cell gives the answer.

The cost is the size of the state space: m·n·(k + 1). One more trick: if k ≥ m + n − 3, the answer is m + n − 2 right away — a shortest path has at most m + n − 3 intermediate cells, and you can break them all. So BFS is needed only for k < m + n − 3, and there are at most 40·40·77 ≈ 1.2·10⁵ states.
cards/6/task: Step through #1293 on the 5×3 grid from the problem statement, k = 1. A state is a cell plus the remaining breaks: the number in a cell is the step on which it was first reached, the small numbers in the corner are the reserves it was reached with. The rig will ask twice what the code does.
cards/6/goal/asks/0/options/0/label: Add (0, 0)·0 and (2, 0)·0: with reserve 0 these states haven't been seen
cards/6/goal/asks/0/options/2/label: Break the wall (1, 1) to the right and add (1, 1)·0
cards/6/goal/asks/0/q: Next, (1, 0)·0 is popped — it was reached by breaking a wall. Above it is the start (0, 0), visited with reserve 1. What does the code do?
cards/6/goal/asks/0/explain: seen looks at the whole triple: (0, 0)·1 has been seen, but (0, 0)·0 hasn't, so it's a new state. A useless one — the cell was already visited with reserve 1, but this code doesn't notice that (how to prune such states comes later in the lesson). To the right is a wall and the reserve is 0: left = −1, no move. Below is the empty (2, 0) — the state (2, 0)·0.
cards/6/goal/asks/1/options/0/label: The neighbor below, (4, 2), is the target: return 6
cards/6/goal/asks/1/options/1/label: (4, 2) is the target, but BFS finishes the level in case there's a shorter path
cards/6/goal/asks/1/q: Next, (3, 2)·0 is popped at step 5: this cell was reached by breaking a wall. What does the code do?
cards/6/goal/asks/1/explain: (4, 2) is an empty cell, no break is needed, left = 0. It's the target, so the code returns steps = 6 right away. Nothing shorter is possible: BFS goes level by level, and every path of 5 steps or fewer has already been explored. Reserve 0 forbids only steps onto walls.
cards/7/q: On the grid [[0,1],[0,0],[1,1],[1,0]] with k = 1 the code returns −1, but the answer is 4. Tap the line with the bug.
cards/7/explain: The mark is per cell, not per state. Step 1: break the wall (0, 1) — state (0, 1)·0 — and go down to (1, 0)·1. Step 2: (0, 1)·0 reaches (1, 1) first and marks the cell. (1, 0)·1, with its unused break, is no longer let into (1, 1) — yet only it could later break the wall (2, 1) and reach the corner in 4 steps. It needs bool[rows, cols, k + 1].
cards/8/title: As many states, as much work
cards/8/body:
Before writing a BFS over states, count them: time and memory are on the order of the number of states times the moves out of each. Up to 10⁶–10⁷ BFS passes; beyond that you need a heuristic or a different idea.

Sliding Puzzle (#773): a 2×3 board, tiles 1–5 and an empty cell; a move slides an adjacent tile into the gap. The state is the whole board as a string like "412503". There are 6! = 720 arrangements, and 360 are reachable from a given one: BFS is instant. The 3×3 puzzle has 9!/2 = 181,440 states, still BFS. But 4×4 has 16!/2 ≈ 10¹³: that needs A* with a heuristic (u12.l3).

Keys and doors (#864): a state is a cell plus the set of collected keys. The set is stored as a mask: bit i of keys is 1 if key i is collected — keys | (1 << i) adds a key, (keys >> i & 1) == 1 checks one. With K keys there are 2ᴷ masks, and cells · 2ᴷ states.

Pruning. Sometimes some states can be thrown away up front. In #1293 BFS yields states in order of steps, and if a cell was already reached with no smaller reserve, the new state is no better. Keep the best reserve each cell was reached with, and accept a state only if its reserve is larger: memory is m·n instead of m·n·(k + 1).

Unity. Puzzles — sliding tiles, Sokoban, switches — are checked for solvability with the same BFS in the editor: a level generator discards unsolvable levels and learns the minimum number of moves for star ratings along the way.
cards/9/q: A puzzle: a 20×20 grid, 3 keys and 3 doors on the level, each door opened by its own key. You need the shortest path to the exit. What is the state, and how many are there?
cards/9/options/0: (cell, key mask): 400 · 2³ = 3200 states, visited is bool[400, 8]
cards/9/options/1: Just the cell: 400 states, with the keys kept in the queue item
cards/9/options/2: (cell, order the keys were collected in): 400 · 3! = 2400 states
cards/9/explain: Future moves depend on where you stand and which doors you can open — that is, on the cell and the set of keys. A set of three keys has 8 masks. The collection order affects nothing: holding keys 1 and 2 is the same whichever was found first.
cards/9/wrong/1: The queue item does carry the keys, but marking by cell discards a repeat visit with a new key — the same bug as with breaks in #1293.
cards/9/wrong/2: The collection order distinguishes states that behave identically: doors open by the set of keys, not by history. Extra states are extra work for nothing.
cards/10/body:
If both the start and the target are known and moves are reversible, BFS can run from both ends: one front grows from the start, the other from the target, and the answer is found when the fronts meet.

Why it's faster. With branching b and distance d, a plain BFS expands on the order of bᵈ vertices, and two opposing ones b^(d/2) each. For b = 10 and d = 6 that's 10⁶ versus 2·10³. To keep the fronts from growing needlessly, always grow the smaller one.

Where it works. Word Ladder: the “one letter” edge is symmetric. Sliding Puzzle: any move can be undone. In #1293 it's awkward: the target cell may be reached with any reserve, so it's unclear which state the backward front should start from — use a plain BFS there.

Fronts are handy to keep in a HashSet: “they met” is a check of the candidate in the opposite set in O(1).
cards/10/deep:
Patterns instead of 26 letters. Word Ladder has a third way to find neighbors: a “pattern → words” dictionary, where a pattern is a word with one letter replaced by *: h*t → [hot, hit]. Building it takes N·L patterns, and a word's neighbors are the union of L lists. It pays off when the alphabet is large (Unicode rather than 26 letters).

Allocations. Every candidate is a new string: for N = 5000 and L = 10 that's 1.3·10⁶ strings, all garbage. In hot code words are encoded as numbers: for L ≤ 12 a word of 26 letters fits in a long at 5 bits per letter, a candidate is made by replacing 5 bits, and a HashSet<long> produces no garbage.

Dominance in #1293, in code. Fill a best[r, c] array with −1, set the start best[0, 0] = k, and instead of seen[y, x, left] check left <= best[y, x]. Why no answer is lost: a state with the same or a larger reserve came on the same or an earlier level, and everything reachable for the new one is reachable for it too. Useless states like (0, 0)·0 from the rig then never appear at all.

When BFS over states isn't enough. With 10¹⁰ states or more — the 4×4 puzzle, Sokoban on a big level — you need a heuristic search (A*, IDA*) or a way to split the problem. That's u12.
cards/11/q: Branching b = 10, the shortest path is d = 6 moves. Roughly how many vertices do plain and bidirectional BFS expand?
cards/11/options/1: ≈ 10⁶ and ≈ 5·10⁵: two fronts mean half the work
cards/11/explain: A plain BFS to depth 6 expands on the order of 10⁶ vertices. Two opposing fronts each reach depth 3: 10³ + 10³. The gain isn't a factor of two but a square root: bᵈ versus 2·b^(d/2).
cards/11/wrong/1: The work grows exponentially with depth, so half the depth means the square root of the work, not half of it.
cards/11/wrong/2: Each level expands not b vertices but b times more than the previous level: 10, 100, 1000…
cards/12/q: You are solving #1293 out loud. Put the steps of the explanation in order.
cards/12/items/0: Clarify: side neighbors, the start and target are empty, what to return without a path
cards/12/items/1: Notice: fewest steps without weights means BFS, but visited per cell loses visits with a larger reserve
cards/12/items/2: Idea: the state (r, c, breaks left), a step onto a wall spends one
cards/12/items/3: Code: level-order BFS, seen[r, c, rem], the answer is the first entry into the target
cards/12/items/4: Run an example where arriving early at a cell wastes a break
cards/12/items/5: Complexity: O(m·n·k), and for k ≥ m + n − 3 the answer is m + n − 2 at once
cards/12/items/6: Improvement: keep the best reserve per cell instead of all k + 1 layers
cards/12/explain: First the agreement on the statement, then the pattern (BFS) and why its naive marking breaks, the idea of a state, the code, a counterexample as a check, the cost with the cutoff on k, and an answer to “can you save memory”.
cards/13/q: Match the problem to its state.
cards/13/pairs/0/1: A word; neighbors are 26 letters per position
cards/13/pairs/2/1: The board as a string, 360 reachable
